```{bash}
#| eval: false
got remote add origin https://github.com/marilounavelet/base-R-2026.git

```

## Variables

A variable is the name of a data manipulated by R. 

```{r}
foo <- 2.5
```

Three parts:

1) `foo`: name of the variable
2) `<-`: assignment operator (on the left the variable name, on the right the 
  value). If you have bad taste, you can replace it by `=`
3) `2.5`: the value

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| include: false
foo = 2.5
```

Basic numerical operations.

```{r}
12 / 4
```

Everywhere I would use a value, I can use instead a variable if the value of
the variable is compatible with what is expected. 

```{r}
foo * 2
```

### Types

Values (and therefore variables) have types. A type specifies what values are
possible (like integers versus real numbers) and what operations can be computed
on the values.

- real numbers `2.5`, `-1.35e-3`
- integers `135L` (for 135)
- logical values `TRUE` and `FALSE`
- strings (small texts) `"bla bla bla bla"` (between single or double quotes)
- functions (to be covered later)

```{r}
135L / 2L
2.5 > -1.2
```

```{r}
1/0
1/(-0)
12/Inf
Inf > 1e250
Inf - Inf
```

```{r}
typeof(foo)
typeof(TRUE)
typeof(135L)
typeof(135)
typeof("a text")
typeof(typeof)
typeof(class)
```

## Vector creation tools 

### Sequences
```{r}
c(1, 2, 3, 4)
# pb : not integers, long to do, pt stocker bcp d'info si on va de 1 à 1M
```



```{r}
1:10 
typeof(1:3)
typeof(c(1, 2, 3))
```

```{r}
-3:10
10:2
```

Alternative, the 'seq' function. 

```{r}
seq(-3, 10)
seq(10,2)
```

Slightly more flexible. 

```{r}
seq(1, 27, 3)
# on peut décider d'un pas (ici 3)
typeof(seq(1, 3))
```

Beware of inconsistent arguments. 

```{r}
#seq(1, 5, -1)
# not working, ici le pas doit être positif 
```

```{r}
seq(from = 0, to = -5, by = -0.5)
```

```{r}
seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 10)
```

Basic application example. 

```{r}
x = seq(from = -pi, to = pi, length.out = 101)
df_sin = data.frame(x = x) |>
  mutate(y = sin(exp(x)))
ggplot(df_sin, aes(x,y))+ 
  geom_line()
```

## Vectorized calculation 
### Simple case 
```{r}
x = c(1, 2, 3)
2*x
x +5
sin(x)
```

### Automatic extension

```{r}
(1:4) + (1:2)
(1:4) + (1:3)
# le second vecteur s'est "dupliqué" pour que les tailles correspondent et que l'addition puisse se faire. 
```

When 'x' and 'y' have different lengths, the short vector is duplicated sufficiently to become as long as the longest. In the example above, '1:2' is expanded into 'c(1, 2, 1, 2)'. 
This is used even if one vector is of length 1, wich explains how '1:4 + 1' works. 

All of that is used internally in dplyr for instance in 'mutate'. 

```{r}
df_demo = data.frame(x = 1:3)
df_demo |> mutate(y = x + 2)
```

```{r}
df_demo2 = data.frame(x = 1:6)
df_demo2 |> mutate(y = x + 1:2)
```

```{r}
x = 1:10
sum(x) ## aggregation function: turns a vector of arbitrary length into a number 
x/sum(x)
```

'x/sum(x)' proceeds as follows:

1) R computes 'sum(x)' -> a vector of length 1
1) 'sum(x)' is expanded into a vector of the length of x, with only identcal values 
3) R computes the division component by component 

'x = 1:3':

1) 'sum(x)' -> 6
2) 6 -> c(6, 6, 6)
3) 'x/c(6, 6, 6)' -> 'c(1/6, 2/6, 3/6)'


## Advanced indexing 

```{r}
x = 3:9
x[2]
```

```{r}
x
x[2:4] # on veut voir les éléments de 2 à 4
x[seq(1, length(x), by = 2)] # on veut voir les éléments de 1 à la fin de la length mais avec un pas de 2
```

In general, 'x[y]' is interpreted the following way:
1) if 'y' contains integer values, they are interpreted as indexed in 'x'
2) if 'y' contains logical values, 'x[i]' is included in the output if 'y[i]' is 'TRUE'

```{r}
x = seq(-5, 11, by = 2)
x
x[c(#-1, 
  0, 3, 1, 2, 5,# -2
   10)]
x > 0
x[x > 0]
x[c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)] # affiche les TRu, comme le vecteur est de longueur 3 pour être appliqué à un vecteur 9, il se répète 3 fois 
x # ça n'a pas modifié x
```

## High level operations on vectors 

### Statistics and aggregation operators 

'min()', 'max()', 'mean()', etc. 

### Ordering and matching 

```{r}
x = 10:-5
x
sort(x)
```

```{r}
y = sample(1:10) # choiit un ordre aléatoire pour les valeurs du vecteur 
y 
sort(y)
sort(y, decreasing = TRUE)
```

```{r}
x = 10:-5
x
order(x) # donne l'indice de l'élément dans le vecteur d'origine à mettre à telle place pr que le vecteur d'origine soit trié dans l'ordre croissant 
x[order(x)]
```

```{r}
y = sample(1:10)
y
order(y) # donne l'indice de l'élément dans le vecteur d'origine à mettre à telle place pr que le vecteur d'origine soit trié dans l'ordre croissant 
y[order(y)]
```
